A 37-year-old carpenter presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe chest pain
that began while climbing stairs an hour ago. He describes the pain as ripping in nature with radiation
to his back. His medical history includes a monitored heart murmur, but he takes no medications. He is
monogamous, denies intravenous drug use, and has not traveled recently. Physical examination
reveals a tall patient in moderate distress with joint hypermobility. His vital signs show: temperature
98.7°F (37.4°C), blood pressure 165/94 mmHg, pulse 148/min, and respirations 12/min. He has equal
bilateral breath sounds and diminished distal pulses. Which finding is most likely to be present in this
patient? Answer Choices: (A) Early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border (B) Late systolic
crescendo murmur at the apex with mid-systolic click (C) Harsh systolic murmur at the left upper
sternal border (D) Holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla (E) Systolic ejection murmur at the right
second intercostal space (F) Continuous machinery murmur at the left infraclavicular region (G)
Mid-systolic click without a murmur (H) Mid-diastolic murmur at the left lower sternal border (I) Opening
snap with a diastolic rumble at the apex (J) Pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border
 A. Mid-systolic click without a murmur
B. Harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border
C. Opening snap with a diastolic rumble at the apex
D. Late systolic crescendo murmur at the apex with mid-systolic click
E. Early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border
F. Continuous machinery murmur at the left infraclavicular region
G. Pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border
H. Systolic ejection murmur at the right second intercostal space
I. Holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla
J. Mid-diastolic murmur at the left lower sternal border
